opus-5.5.text:
I'd actually push back a little on the framing of "competitive advantage," because I don't think of what we do as competing with the big model companies head-on. They have enormous compute, huge engineering teams, and they're optimizing for a product: a model that works really well at scale. We can't win that game, and honestly I don't think academia should try.

What we can do is ask a different kind of question. The Physics of AI idea is basically this: treat neural networks the way physicists treat natural phenomena. Instead of only asking "how do we make the loss go down," we ask "what is actually happening inside? What are the mechanisms, the phases, the laws?" Things like grokking, representation formation, scaling behavior. These are phenomena, and phenomena deserve explanations.

Physics has a particular methodology for that, and I think it's an underused one in AI. You find the simplest toy setting where the phenomenon still shows up, you strip away everything that isn't essential, and you try to build an intuitive or even quantitative theory. A lot of that work can be done on a laptop or a few GPUs. So the constraint of small compute actually pushes us toward cleaner experiments, and sometimes cleaner insight.

So if there's an "advantage," it's more about freedom and perspective. Big companies have strong incentives to chase the next benchmark or the next release. We have the luxury of being curious, of spending months on a question that might look useless in the short term, like why a tiny network suddenly generalizes after memorizing, and that understanding can eventually feed back into how people design architectures or training recipes. KAN came partly from that mindset too: asking whether we could build networks that are more interpretable and closer to how scientists think about functions.

I see it as complementary. They're building the engines; we're trying to write the thermodynamics. Historically, you needed both. The steam engine came first, but the theory of thermodynamics is what let people understand the limits and design much better engines. I'd like our lab to play some small role like that for AI.

r001.rationale: The response says small-scale experiments can yield cleaner insights, but does not state that AI can accelerate research into the Physics of AI.

r002.rationale: It describes large companies’ focus on benchmarks and product releases, but does not say they view the Physics of AI route as excessively risky or present that perception as an opportunity.

r003.rationale: The response attributes companies’ priorities to their product incentives, not to a lack of belief in the Physics of AI route.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd push back a little on the word "competitive," because I don't really see us as competing with large model companies. They have thousands of GPUs and hundreds of engineers; a university lab like mine cannot and should not try to build the next frontier model. If we tried to play their game, we'd lose by default.

What we can do is ask different questions. A big lab is under enormous pressure to ship. When something works, they scale it; when something breaks, they patch it. There's very little room to stop and ask why. The Physics of AI approach is exactly that pause. We treat a neural network the way a physicist treats a new material: you build small, controlled systems, you vary one parameter at a time, you look for phase transitions, scaling laws, conserved quantities, and you try to write down a minimal theory that explains what you see. Grokking is a good example. It looks like a weird curiosity, but once you study it in toy settings you start to see it as a signal about how representations form, and that tells you something about training dynamics in general.

The advantage, if you want to call it that, is that understanding compounds differently from compute. Compute buys you capability today. Understanding sometimes buys you a shortcut that nobody with more compute would have found, because they weren't looking. KAN came out of thinking about the Kolmogorov-Arnold theorem, not from scaling anything. Whether it ends up mattering at scale is still an open question, and I'm honest about that, but it's the kind of idea that only appears when you let yourself be curious about structure instead of just performance.

I'd also say the field needs both. Physics didn't progress only through big experiments at CERN; it also needed people doing tabletop experiments and writing down equations. Right now AI has a lot of CERN and not enough tabletop. So I think of our lab less as a competitor and more as part of the ecosystem that the large companies ultimately benefit from. Some of my students will go work there, and they'll bring this way of thinking with them. That's a good outcome.

r001.rationale: The response describes using Physics of AI to study neural networks, but does not say AI can accelerate research into Physics of AI.

r002.rationale: It says large companies face pressure to ship, but does not identify their view of the Physics of AI route as excessively risky or that view as an opportunity for Liu’s lab.

r003.rationale: It attributes limited exploration to pressure to ship and little room to ask why, not to companies’ lack of belief in the Physics of AI route.

astra-6.text:
I think our advantage is that we can ask a different kind of question. A large model company has to build a system that performs well across many tasks. We can focus on understanding why learning works, what structures emerge inside a model, and which principles carry across different settings.

That’s what the physics perspective brings: you look for a simple setting that captures an important phenomenon, then try to find an explanation you can test. A smaller experiment can be valuable if it helps you distinguish between competing explanations.

So I wouldn’t frame it as competing with large companies on scale. Our opportunity is to develop understanding that leads to different ways of building models. If that understanding helps us make learning more efficient or models easier to interpret, then a small lab can make a meaningful contribution without having the largest compute budget.

r001.rationale: The response discusses studying learning through a physics perspective, but does not say AI can accelerate research into the Physics of AI.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe large model companies as viewing the Physics of AI route as excessively risky or present that view as an opportunity for the lab.

r003.rationale: The response does not attribute any lack of investment in the Physics of AI route to companies disbelieving in it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think our advantage is that we’re trying to answer a different kind of question. Large model companies are very good at building systems and pushing performance. With a Physics of AI approach, we ask: What are the underlying principles? Can we find a simple model that explains an important behavior, and then use that understanding to make better predictions or design better methods?

For a small lab, choosing the right question is crucial. We can’t compete by doing the same experiment at a larger scale. But we can study a phenomenon in a controlled setting, identify what matters, and test whether that insight carries over to more complex systems.

Of course, a beautiful explanation isn’t enough—it has to survive experiments. The opportunity is to turn understanding into something useful. I see that as complementary to the work of large companies, while giving us a distinct direction.

r001.rationale: The response describes using underlying principles to improve predictions and methods, but does not say AI can accelerate research into the Physics of AI.

r002.rationale: It says the approach gives the lab a distinct direction complementary to large companies, but does not identify their view of the route as excessively risky.

r003.rationale: The response does not attribute large companies’ lack of investment to a lack of belief in the Physics of AI route.
